title: Κύκλωπος σπέος
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still telling his story at the court of the Phaeacians, picks twelve of his best companions and goes up from the ship to the Cyclops' cave, carrying a skin of dark wine given him by Maron, the priest of Apollo at Ismarus whom Odysseus' men spared when they sacked the town, and a wine so strong that a single cup took twenty measures of water. The cave is empty, and the men gaze at the racks of cheese, the pens of lambs and kids, and the pails full of whey. His companions beg him to take the cheeses and the young animals and sail off, but he refuses, wanting to see the owner and hoping for a guest-gift. The Cyclops comes home with a load of dry wood, drives his flocks in, shuts the door with a stone that twenty-two wagons could not shift, milks his animals and lights a fire, and sees the strangers. He asks who they are and whether they are pirates. Odysseus answers that they are Achaeans of Agamemnon's host, driven off course, and begs for a guest-gift in the name of Zeus, protector of suppliants and guests. The Cyclops mocks him: the Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus, and he would spare no one unless his own heart bade him. He asks where the ship is moored.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε τοὺς ἄλλους κελόμην ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους
αὐτοῦ πὰρ νηί τε μένειν καὶ νῆα ἔρυσθαι,
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ κρίνας ἑτάρων δυοκαίδεκ’ ἀρίστους
βῆν·
sentences.tr:
dē tote tous allous kelomēn eriēras hetairous
autou par nēi te menein kai nēa erysthai,
autar egō krinas hetarōn dyokaidek’ aristous
bēn·
sentences.l:
Then indeed the others I ordered, my trusty companions,
there by the ship to stay and the ship to guard,
but I, having picked out of my companions the twelve best,
went;
sentences.i: Then I told the rest of my trusty companions to stay right there by the ship and guard it, while I picked out the twelve best of my companions and set out;
sentences.n: τοὺς ἄλλους … ἑταίρους is the object of κελόμην 'I ordered', an unaugmented imperfect of κέλομαι, and the infinitives μένειν 'to stay' and ἔρυσθαι 'to guard' (from ἐρύομαι 'protect') give the order; ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι is 'trusty companions', though the sense of ἐρίηρος is not fully known. αὐτοῦ, with the circumflex, is the adverb 'on the spot'. αὐτάρ 'but' sets the men chosen against the men left behind. κρίνας means 'having picked out', δυοκαίδεκα is 'twelve' (two and ten), and βῆν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω 'go'. Odysseus is still telling his story at the Phaeacian court: the speech that opened at 9.2 runs on, so this unit carries no quotation mark.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ αἴγεον ἀσκὸν ἔχον μέλανος οἴνοιο
ἡδέος, ὅν μοι ἔδωκε Μάρων, Ἐυάνθεος υἱός,
ἱρεὺς Ἀπόλλωνος, ὃς Ἴσμαρον ἀμφιβεβήκει,
sentences.tr:
atar aigeon askon echon melanos oinoio
hēdeos, hon moi edōke Marōn, Eyantheos huios,
hireus Apollōnos, hos Ismaron amphibebēkei,
sentences.l:
and yet a goat-skin I had, of dark wine,
sweet, which to me gave Maron, Euanthes’ son,
priest of Apollo, who had watched over Ismarus,
sentences.i: I also had a goat-skin of dark, sweet wine, which Maron, son of Euanthes, had given me; he was priest of Apollo and watched over Ismarus,
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is another 'but, and yet', like αὐτάρ. ἔχον is an imperfect, 'I had with me', and αἴγεον ἀσκόν is 'a goat-skin', used as a wine-skin; μέλανος οἴνοιο and ἡδέος are genitives of what it held, 'of dark, sweet wine'. ὅν is the relative 'which', not the possessive, with μοι 'to me'; Ἐυάνθεος υἱός is 'son of Euanthes', and ἱρεύς is Ionic ἱερεύς 'priest'. ἀμφιβεβήκει is the pluperfect of ἀμφιβαίνω, 'go about, stand over', said of a protector, so the priest watched over Ismarus, the city of the Cicones. The next unit gives the reason for the gift.

sentences.t:
οὕνεκά μιν σὺν παιδὶ περισχόμεθ’ ἠδὲ γυναικὶ
ἁζόμενοι·
sentences.tr:
houneka min syn paidi perischometh’ ēde gynaiki
hazomenoi·
sentences.l:
because him, with child and wife, we shielded,
reverencing;
sentences.i: because, out of reverence, we shielded him along with his son and his wife;
sentences.n: οὕνεκα is 'because' (= ὅτι), and μιν 'him' is Maron. περισχόμεθ’ is the aorist middle of περιέχω 'hold round, shield'; σὺν παιδί and ἠδὲ γυναικί 'with his child and his wife' name the others who were spared with him. ἁζόμενοι is a participle of ἄζομαι 'stand in awe of, revere', with no object of its own: the γάρ clause that follows names the grove of Apollo, and that is what the men revered. The ano teleia falls after ἁζόμενοι, the first word of line 200.

sentences.t:
ᾤκει γὰρ ἐν ἄλσεϊ δενδρήεντι
Φοίβου Ἀπόλλωνος.
sentences.tr:
ōikei gar en alseï dendrēenti
Phoibou Apollōnos.
sentences.l:
for he lived in a grove, tree-filled,
of Phoebus Apollo.
sentences.i: for he lived in the tree-filled grove of Phoebus Apollo.
sentences.n: ᾤκει is the contracted imperfect of οἰκέω 'live', and γάρ gives the reason for the sparing. ἄλσος is a sacred grove, here in the dative ἄλσεϊ, and δενδρήεντι 'tree-filled' is built on δένδρον 'tree'. Φοίβου Ἀπόλλωνος is a genitive, 'of Phoebus Apollo': Φοῖβος is a title of Apollo, understood by the usual explanation as 'bright'. The unit ends mid-line, after the full stop, and the rest of 201 opens the next.

sentences.t: ὁ δέ μοι πόρεν ἀγλαὰ δῶρα·
sentences.tr: ho de moi poren aglaa dōra·
sentences.l: and he to me gave splendid gifts:
sentences.i: And he gave me splendid gifts:
sentences.n: ὁ is the pronoun 'he', and μοι 'to me'. πόρεν is the unaugmented aorist of πόρω 'give, grant', a poetic verb beside ἔδωκε and δῶκε in the lines that follow. ἀγλαά 'splendid' agrees with δῶρα 'gifts'; the ano teleia promises the list that the next unit supplies.

sentences.t:
χρυσοῦ μέν μοι ἔδωκ’ ἐυεργέος ἑπτὰ τάλαντα,
δῶκε δέ μοι κρητῆρα πανάργυρον, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
οἶνον ἐν ἀμφιφορεῦσι δυώδεκα πᾶσιν ἀφύσσας
ἡδὺν ἀκηράσιον, θεῖον ποτόν·
sentences.tr:
chrysou men moi edōk’ eyergeos hepta talanta,
dōke de moi krētēra panargyron, autar epeita
oinon en amphiphoreusi dyōdeka pasin aphyssas
hēdyn akērasion, theion poton·
sentences.l:
Of gold, on the one hand, to me he gave, well-made, seven talents,
and he gave me a mixing-bowl all of silver, and then
wine, in amphoras, twelve, all of them, having drawn,
sweet, unmixed, a divine drink;
sentences.i: He gave me seven talents of well-made gold and a mixing-bowl all of silver, and then wine — he drew it off into twelve jars, filling them all — sweet and unmixed, a divine drink;
sentences.n: The gifts are a run of accusatives after ἔδωκ’ and δῶκε 'gave'. τάλαντα are talents, a unit of weight whose size in Homer is uncertain; ἐυεργέος 'well-made' agrees with χρυσοῦ 'of gold'. A κρητήρ is the bowl in which wine and water are mixed (compare line 210), and πανάργυρον means 'all of silver'. οἶνον … ἀφύσσας is 'having drawn off wine', the aorist participle of ἀφύσσω 'draw a liquid', into twelve ἀμφιφορεῦσι 'amphoras, two-handled jars', with πᾶσιν 'all of them'. ἀκηράσιον 'unmixed', undiluted, is why the water of line 209 is needed; θεῖον is 'divine'.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις αὐτὸν
ἠείδη δμώων οὐδ’ ἀμφιπόλων ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
ἀλλ’ αὐτὸς ἄλοχός τε φίλη ταμίη τε μί’ οἴη.
sentences.tr:
oude tis auton
ēeidē dmōōn oud’ amphipolōn eni oikōi,
all’ autos alochos te philē tamiē te mi’ oiē.
sentences.l:
and not anyone it
knew, of the servants or of the attendants in the house,
but he himself and his dear wife and one housekeeper alone.
sentences.i: and none of the servants or attendants in the house knew of it, only he himself and his dear wife and a single housekeeper.
sentences.n: ἠείδη is a Homeric past of οἶδα (Attic ᾔδη 'he knew'), and its object αὐτόν 'it' is the wine, so 'no one knew it' means no one knew of it. τις stands with the genitives δμώων 'of the servants' and ἀμφιπόλων 'of the attendants'. ἀλλά 'but' brings three nominatives that name the ones who did know: αὐτός 'he himself', that is Maron, ἄλοχος 'wife' with φίλη 'dear', and ταμίη 'housekeeper'. μί’ οἴη is μία οἴη 'one alone'.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὅτε πίνοιεν μελιηδέα οἶνον ἐρυθρόν,
ἓν δέπας ἐμπλήσας ὕδατος ἀνὰ εἴκοσι μέτρα
χεῦ’, ὀδμὴ δ’ ἡδεῖα ἀπὸ κρητῆρος ὀδώδει
θεσπεσίη·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ hote pinoien meliēdea oinon erythron,
hen depas emplēsas hydatos ana eikosi metra
cheu’, odmē d’ hēdeia apo krētēros odōdei
thespesiē·
sentences.l:
And this, whenever they drank honey-sweet red wine,
one cup having filled, to twenty measures of water
he poured, and a smell, sweet, from the mixing-bowl was coming
wondrous;
sentences.i: Whenever they drank that honey-sweet red wine, he would fill one cup of it and pour it into twenty measures of water, and a sweet smell would come from the mixing-bowl, a wondrous one;
sentences.n: τόν is a pronoun, 'it', the wine, with μελιηδέα οἶνον ἐρυθρόν 'honey-sweet red wine' in apposition. ὅτε with the optative πίνοιεν means 'whenever they drank': a habit, so English wants 'would'. In ἐμπλήσας … χεῦ’ 'having filled … he poured' the wine is understood as what is filled and poured, and the subject is whoever did the pouring; ὕδατος 'of water' depends on μέτρα, not on ἐμπλήσας, and ἀνά with the accusative εἴκοσι μέτρα gives the proportion, 'to twenty measures'. The construction is compressed, and a cup to twenty measures of water is a very heavy dilution. ὀδώδει is a pluperfect of ὄζω used as an imperfect, 'was giving off a smell', and θεσπεσίη 'wondrous' opens line 211, running over from 210, and agrees with ὀδμή.

sentences.t: τότ’ ἂν οὔ τοι ἀποσχέσθαι φίλον ἦεν.
sentences.tr: tot’ an ou toi aposchesthai philon ēen.
sentences.l: then, you know, not to hold back was pleasing.
sentences.i: Then, I tell you, no one would have liked to hold back.
sentences.n: τότ’ is τότε 'then', and τοι is a dative 'to you', an appeal to the hearer, 'I tell you'. ἀποσχέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀπέχω, 'hold oneself off, abstain', and φίλον ἦεν is 'was dear, was pleasing'; ἂν with the imperfect ἦεν makes it 'would have been'. The negative οὔ covers the whole clause: it was not pleasant to abstain.

sentences.t:
τοῦ φέρον ἐμπλήσας ἀσκὸν μέγαν, ἐν δὲ καὶ ᾖα
κωρύκῳ·
sentences.tr:
tou pheron emplēsas askon megan, en de kai ēia
kōrykōi·
sentences.l:
Of this I carried, having filled, a great skin, and in also provisions
in a leather bag;
sentences.i: I filled a great skin with some of this and carried it, and provisions too in a leather bag;
sentences.n: τοῦ is a partitive genitive, 'some of it', the wine; φέρον is an unaugmented imperfect, 'I was carrying', and ἐμπλήσας 'having filled' takes ἀσκὸν μέγαν 'a great skin'. ἐν δὲ καὶ ᾖα κωρύκῳ is 'and in a leather bag also provisions': ᾖα is taken as the neuter plural ἠία 'provisions for a journey' (the same letters can also spell the imperfect of εἶμι 'go', which cannot be meant with a bag to carry things in), and ἐν … κωρύκῳ 'in a leather bag' has ᾖα standing between the preposition and its noun. The ano teleia falls after κωρύκῳ, early in line 213.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα γάρ μοι ὀίσατο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
ἄνδρ’ ἐπελεύσεσθαι μεγάλην ἐπιειμένον ἀλκήν,
ἄγριον, οὔτε δίκας ἐὺ εἰδότα οὔτε θέμιστας.
sentences.tr:
autika gar moi oisato thymos agēnōr
andr’ epeleusesthai megalēn epieimenon alkēn,
agrion, oute dikas ey eidota oute themistas.
sentences.l:
for at once to me foreboded my manly spirit
that a man would come upon us, clothed in great might,
savage, neither justice well knowing nor rules of right.
sentences.i: for my proud spirit at once foreboded that a man would come upon us, clothed in great might, savage, with no good knowledge of justice or of rules of right.
sentences.n: θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ 'manly spirit' is the subject of ὀίσατο, the aorist middle of ὀΐομαι 'suspect, have a foreboding', which takes an accusative and infinitive: ἄνδρ’ ἐπελεύσεσθαι 'that a man would come upon (us)', ἐπελεύσεσθαι being a future infinitive. ἐπιειμένον, a perfect middle participle of ἐπιέννυμι 'clothe', means 'clothed in', with ἀλκήν 'might' as what he wears: strength pictured as a garment. ἄγριον is 'savage', and οὔτε … οὔτε 'neither … nor' governs ἐὺ εἰδότα 'well knowing' with two objects, δίκας 'justice' and θέμιστας 'rules of right' (compare 112 in the previous part).

sentences.t:
καρπαλίμως δ’ εἰς ἄντρον ἀφικόμεθ’, οὐδέ μιν ἔνδον
εὕρομεν, ἀλλ’ ἐνόμευε νομὸν κάτα πίονα μῆλα.
sentences.tr:
karpalimōs d’ eis antron aphikometh’, oude min endon
heuromen, all’ enomeue nomon kata piona mēla.
sentences.l:
Quickly to the cave we came, and him inside
we did not find, but he was pasturing along the pasture fat flocks.
sentences.i: We came quickly to the cave, but did not find him inside: he was out pasturing his fat flocks over the pasture-land.
sentences.n: καρπαλίμως 'quickly' opens the line, and ἀφικόμεθ’ is the aorist of ἀφικνέομαι 'arrive'. μιν 'him' is the owner of the cave, still unnamed, and εὕρομεν 'we found' is an aorist. ἀλλά 'but' says where he was instead: ἐνόμευε is an imperfect of νομεύω 'pasture, tend', with νομὸν κάτα 'along the pasture', κάτα being κατά placed after its noun. πίονα μῆλα is 'fat flocks', μῆλα meaning small livestock, sheep and goats together.

sentences.t: ἐλθόντες δ’ εἰς ἄντρον ἐθηεύμεσθα ἕκαστα.
sentences.tr: elthontes d’ eis antron ethēeumestha hekasta.
sentences.l: And having come into the cave, we gazed at each thing.
sentences.i: Once inside the cave, we gazed at everything.
sentences.n: ἐλθόντες is an aorist participle, 'having come', and ἐθηεύμεσθα is the imperfect of θηέομαι 'gaze at, look at in wonder', with the epic ending -μεσθα for -μεθα; ἕκαστα is 'each thing'. The unit is a pause between the arrival and the inventory that the next units give.

sentences.t:
ταρσοὶ μὲν τυρῶν βρῖθον, στείνοντο δὲ σηκοὶ
ἀρνῶν ἠδ’ ἐρίφων·
sentences.tr:
tarsoi men tyrōn brithon, steinonto de sēkoi
arnōn ēd’ eriphōn·
sentences.l:
Racks, on the one hand, of cheeses were heavy, and were crowded the pens
with lambs and kids;
sentences.i: The racks were heavy with cheeses, and the pens were crowded with lambs and kids;
sentences.n: ταρσοί are wicker racks or crates on which cheeses were laid out to dry, and μέν looks ahead to the δέ that follows. βρῖθον is an unaugmented imperfect of βρίθω 'be heavy', with the genitive τυρῶν 'with cheeses'; στείνοντο is the imperfect of στείνομαι 'be crowded, be packed', and the σηκοί 'pens' are crowded with ἀρνῶν 'lambs' and ἐρίφων 'kids', both genitives, as with βρῖθον.

sentences.t:
διακεκριμέναι δὲ ἕκασται
ἔρχατο, χωρὶς μὲν πρόγονοι, χωρὶς δὲ μέτασσαι,
χωρὶς δ’ αὖθ’ ἕρσαι.
sentences.tr:
diakekrimenai de hekastai
erchato, chōris men progonoi, chōris de metassai,
chōris d’ auth’ hersai.
sentences.l:
and separated, each group,
were shut in, apart the earlier-born, apart the middle ones,
apart again the dews.
sentences.i: Each group was penned by itself: the eldest apart, the middle ones apart, and again the youngest apart.
sentences.n: διακεκριμέναι is a perfect passive participle of διακρίνω 'separate', agreeing with ἕκασται 'each group', and ἔρχατο is the epic pluperfect passive of εἴργω 'shut in', 'had been penned'. χωρίς 'apart' sets out three groups. πρόγονοι means 'those born earlier', the oldest; μέτασσαι is a rare word, and 'the middle ones' is a guess from its form (μετά 'between') and the sense; ἕρσαι is 'dews', which the ancient commentators take as a figure for the newest born. The sense of the last two words is not certain.

sentences.t:
ναῖον δ’ ὀρῷ ἄγγεα πάντα,
γαυλοί τε σκαφίδες τε, τετυγμένα, τοῖς ἐνάμελγεν.
sentences.tr:
naion d’ orōi angea panta,
gauloi te skaphides te, tetygmena, tois enamelgen.
sentences.l:
and were awash with whey the vessels all,
pails and bowls, wrought, into which he milked.
sentences.i: and all the vessels, the pails and bowls, well-wrought, that he milked into, were awash with whey.
sentences.n: ναῖον is an imperfect of a verb 'flow, be awash', with the dative ὀρῷ 'with whey', the watery part that is left when milk curdles; its subject is ἄγγεα πάντα 'all the vessels'. γαυλοί 'pails' and σκαφίδες 'bowls' name the vessels, and τετυγμένα, a perfect passive participle of τεύχω 'make', is the word of craftsmanship, 'wrought'. τοῖς ἐνάμελγεν is 'into which he milked': τοῖς is a relative pronoun, and ἐνάμελγεν an imperfect of ἐναμέλγω 'milk into'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἐμὲ μὲν πρώτισθ’ ἕταροι λίσσοντ’ ἐπέεσσιν
τυρῶν αἰνυμένους ἰέναι πάλιν, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
καρπαλίμως ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν ἐρίφους τε καὶ ἄρνας
σηκῶν ἐξελάσαντας ἐπιπλεῖν ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ·
sentences.tr:
enth’ eme men prōtisth’ hetaroi lissont’ epeessin
tyrōn ainymenous ienai palin, autar epeita
karpalimōs epi nēa thoēn eriphous te kai arnas
sēkōn exelasantas epiplein halmyron hydōr·
sentences.l:
There me indeed first of all my companions begged with words
cheeses taking to go back, but then
quickly to the swift ship the kids and the lambs
from the pens having driven out, to sail over the salt water;
sentences.i: There my companions first of all begged me to take some of the cheeses and go back, and then to drive the kids and lambs out of the pens, hurry down to the swift ship, and sail away over the salt water;
sentences.n: ἐμὲ μὲν πρώτισθ’ is 'me, first of all': ἐμέ is the object of λίσσοντ’, an unaugmented imperfect of λίσσομαι 'beg', and πρώτισθ’ is πρώτιστα, a superlative adverb, elided. What they begged is given by two infinitives, ἰέναι 'to go' and ἐπιπλεῖν 'to sail over', with accusative participles, αἰνυμένους 'taking' and ἐξελάσαντας 'having driven out', that agree with an understood 'us'. τυρῶν αἰνυμένους is 'taking some of the cheeses' (a partitive genitive), and σηκῶν is 'from the pens'. ἐρίφους τε καὶ ἄρνας are 'kids and lambs'. ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ 'salt water' is an accusative of the space sailed over.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐ πιθόμην, ἦ τ’ ἂν πολὺ κέρδιον ἦεν,
ὄφρ’ αὐτόν τε ἴδοιμι, καὶ εἴ μοι ξείνια δοίη.
sentences.tr:
all’ egō ou pithomēn, ē t’ an poly kerdion ēen,
ophr’ auton te idoimi, kai ei moi xeinia doiē.
sentences.l:
But I did not obey, — truly much better it would have been, —
so that him I might see, and if to me guest-gifts he might give.
sentences.i: But I did not obey — and it would surely have been far better if I had — for I wanted to see the man himself, and to see whether he would give me guest-gifts.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐ πιθόμην 'but I did not obey' answers the μέν of 224: they begged me, and I refused. πιθόμην is the aorist middle of πείθομαι 'obey'. ἦ τ’ ἂν πολὺ κέρδιον ἦεν is an aside: 'truly it would have been much better', ἂν with the imperfect ἦεν saying what would have been and was not, and κέρδιον being the comparative of κέρδος 'gain', 'more profitable'. ὄφρα with the optatives ἴδοιμι and δοίη gives the purpose: 'so that I might see him, and whether he would give'. ξείνια are the gifts a host gives a guest.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλ’ ἑτάροισι φανεὶς ἐρατεινὸς ἔσεσθαι.
sentences.tr: oud’ ar’ emell’ hetaroisi phaneis erateinos esesthai.
sentences.l: Nor, as it proved, was he going, to my companions when he appeared, to be lovely.
sentences.i: But once he appeared, he was not, as it turned out, going to prove lovely to my companions.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ is 'and not, as it proved'. ἔμελλε 'was going to, was destined to' takes the future infinitive ἔσεσθαι 'to be', and φανείς is the aorist passive participle of φαίνομαι, 'having appeared'; ἑτάροισι is a dative in -οισι, 'to my companions'. ἐρατεινός 'lovely, desirable' is meant grimly, an understatement: Odysseus speaks with what he knows now.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ πῦρ κήαντες ἐθύσαμεν ἠδὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ
τυρῶν αἰνύμενοι φάγομεν, μένομέν τέ μιν ἔνδον
ἥμενοι, ἧος ἐπῆλθε νέμων.
sentences.tr:
entha de pyr kēantes ethysamen ēde kai autoi
tyrōn ainymenoi phagomen, menomen te min endon
hēmenoi, hēos epēlthe nemōn.
sentences.l:
There a fire having kindled we sacrificed, and also ourselves
cheeses taking we ate, and we waited for him inside
sitting, until he came up, shepherding.
sentences.i: There we kindled a fire and made an offering, and ate some of the cheeses ourselves, and sat waiting for him inside until he came up, shepherding his flocks.
sentences.n: κήαντες is an aorist participle of καίω 'burn', and ἐθύσαμεν the aorist of θύω, 'we made a burnt offering'; what was burnt is not said. ἠδὲ καὶ αὐτοί 'and also ourselves' sets the men's own meal against the offering. τυρῶν αἰνύμενοι 'taking some of the cheeses' repeats the phrase of 225, now in the nominative, and φάγομεν 'we ate' is an aorist. μένομεν is an imperfect without augment (its form is the same as the present), 'we waited', with μιν 'for him'. ἧος is the epic ἕως 'until', and ἐπῆλθε νέμων 'came up shepherding' has νέμων, the participle of νέμω 'pasture, tend'.

sentences.t:
φέρε δ’ ὄβριμον ἄχθος
ὕλης ἀζαλέης, ἵνα οἱ ποτιδόρπιον εἴη,
ἔντοσθεν δ’ ἄντροιο βαλὼν ὀρυμαγδὸν ἔθηκεν·
sentences.tr:
phere d’ obrimon achthos
hylēs azaleēs, hina hoi potidorpion eiē,
entosthen d’ antroio balōn orymagdon ethēken·
sentences.i: He was carrying a mighty load of dry wood, so that it would serve as his supper, and he threw it down inside the cave with a crash.
sentences.n: φέρε is an unaugmented imperfect, 'he was carrying', and its subject is the Cyclops, still unnamed. ὄβριμον ἄχθος is 'a mighty load', with ὕλης ἀζαλέης 'of dry wood' as a genitive of material. ἵνα οἱ ποτιδόρπιον εἴη 'so that it might be for his supper': ποτιδόρπιον is built on ποτί (= πρός) 'toward' and δόρπον 'the evening meal', so 'for the evening meal'. βαλών 'having thrown' is an aorist participle, ὀρυμαγδόν an accusative meaning 'a din, a crash', and ἔθηκεν the aorist of τίθημι, 'made'. ἔντοσθεν … ἄντροιο is 'inside the cave'.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς δὲ δείσαντες ἀπεσσύμεθ’ ἐς μυχὸν ἄντρου.
sentences.tr: hēmeis de deisantes apessymeth’ es mychon antrou.
sentences.l: and we, having feared, rushed away into the recess of the cave.
sentences.i: and we, in fear, rushed away to the far end of the cave.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς δέ 'and we' turns the subject from the Cyclops to Odysseus and his men. δείσαντες is an aorist participle of δείδω 'fear', and ἀπεσσύμεθ’ is the aorist middle of ἀποσεύω 'rush away', with the doubled σ of epic verse. μυχός is the innermost part of a cave, 'recess', and ἐς μυχὸν ἄντρου is 'into the recess of the cave'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ εἰς εὐρὺ σπέος ἤλασε πίονα μῆλα
πάντα μάλ’ ὅσσ’ ἤμελγε, τὰ δ’ ἄρσενα λεῖπε θύρηφιν,
ἀρνειούς τε τράγους τε, βαθείης ἔκτοθεν αὐλῆς.
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ eis eury speos ēlase piona mēla
panta mal’ hoss’ ēmelge, ta d’ arsena leipe thyrēphin,
arneious te tragous te, batheiēs ektothen aulēs.
sentences.l:
but he, into the wide cave, drove his fat flocks,
all of them, as many as he milked, and the males he left at the door,
rams and he-goats, outside the deep yard.
sentences.i: Then he drove his fat flocks into the wide cave, all those that he milked, but left the males outside by the door, the rams and the he-goats, beyond the deep yard.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ 'but' turns to the Cyclops, and ὅ γε is 'he', a pronoun. ἤλασε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive', with εὐρὺ σπέος 'the wide cave' and πίονα μῆλα 'fat flocks' as objects; πάντα μάλ’ ὅσσ’ ἤμελγε is 'all of them, as many as he milked'. τὰ δ’ ἄρσενα 'and the males' were left θύρηφιν 'at the door': -φιν is an old ending that marks place, like -θι. ἀρνειούς is 'rams' and τράγους 'he-goats', and βαθείης ἔκτοθεν αὐλῆς 'outside the deep yard' recalls the walled yard of 184–186.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ ἐπέθηκε θυρεὸν μέγαν ὑψόσ’ ἀείρας,
ὄβριμον·
sentences.tr:
autar epeit’ epethēke thyreon megan hypsos’ aeiras,
obrimon·
sentences.l:
But then he set on a great door-stone, having lifted it up high,
mighty;
sentences.i: Then, heaving it up high, he set a great door-stone in place, a mighty one;
sentences.n: θυρεόν is 'a door-stone', a slab of stone that closes a doorway (the word later means a shield). ἐπέθηκε is the aorist of ἐπιτίθημι 'set on', and ὑψόσ’ ἀείρας is 'having lifted it on high', ὑψόσε being an adverb of direction. μέγαν 'great' is the epithet of the stone, and ὄβριμον 'mighty' follows as an afterthought after a pause, the same adjective as in ὄβριμον ἄχθος at 233.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν τόν γε δύω καὶ εἴκοσ’ ἄμαξαι
ἐσθλαὶ τετράκυκλοι ἀπ’ οὔδεος ὀχλίσσειαν·
sentences.tr:
ouk an ton ge dyō kai eikos’ amaxai
esthlai tetrakykloi ap’ oudeos ochlisseian·
sentences.l:
Not it, at least, two and twenty wagons,
good four-wheeled ones, from the ground could heave;
sentences.i: Not even twenty-two good four-wheeled wagons could have heaved it from the ground;
sentences.n: οὐκ ἂν … ὀχλίσσειαν is a potential optative: 'would not be able to heave'. The subject is ἄμαξαι 'wagons', δύω καὶ εἴκοσ’ 'two and twenty' of them, ἐσθλαὶ τετράκυκλοι 'good four-wheeled'; τόν γε 'it, at least' picks up θυρεόν. ὀχλίσσειαν is from ὀχλίζω 'move with a lever, heave', and ἀπ’ οὔδεος is 'from the ground'.

sentences.t: τόσσην ἠλίβατον πέτρην ἐπέθηκε θύρῃσιν.
sentences.tr: tossēn ēlibaton petrēn epethēke thyrēisin.
sentences.l: so great a towering rock he set on the doors.
sentences.i: Such a towering rock did he set against the doorway.
sentences.n: τόσσην 'so great' agrees with πέτρην 'rock', beside ἠλίβατον. The meaning of ἠλίβατος is not known: 'steep, towering' is the traditional guess, and it is followed here. ἐπέθηκε is the same verb as in 240, and θύρῃσιν 'doors' is a plural for a single doorway, a dative. The stone that was called θυρεός is now πέτρη 'rock, crag'.

sentences.t:
ἑζόμενος δ’ ἤμελγεν ὄις καὶ μηκάδας αἶγας,
πάντα κατὰ μοῖραν, καὶ ὑπ’ ἔμβρυον ἧκεν ἑκάστῃ.
sentences.tr:
hezomenos d’ ēmelgen ois kai mēkadas aigas,
panta kata moiran, kai hyp’ embryon hēken hekastēi.
sentences.l:
And sitting down he milked the sheep and the bleating goats,
all according to what is fitting, and under each her young he put.
sentences.i: Sitting down, he milked the sheep and the bleating goats, all as is fitting, and put her young one beneath each.
sentences.n: ἑζόμενος is the participle of ἕζομαι 'sit down', and ἤμελγεν an imperfect, 'he was milking', with ὄις 'sheep' (accusative plural; ewes, since they are milked) and μηκάδας αἶγας 'bleating goats'. πάντα κατὰ μοῖραν is 'all according to what is fitting'. ὑπ’ … ἧκεν is tmesis for the aorist of ὑφίημι 'put under', and ἔμβρυον is 'young one', the lamb or kid, with ἑκάστῃ 'to each', a feminine dative.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἥμισυ μὲν θρέψας λευκοῖο γάλακτος
πλεκτοῖς ἐν ταλάροισιν ἀμησάμενος κατέθηκεν,
ἥμισυ δ’ αὖτ’ ἔστησεν ἐν ἄγγεσιν, ὄφρα οἱ εἴη
πίνειν αἰνυμένῳ καί οἱ ποτιδόρπιον εἴη.
sentences.tr:
autika d’ hēmisy men threpsas leukoio galaktos
plektois en talaroisin amēsamenos katethēken,
hēmisy d’ aut’ estēsen en angesin, ophra hoi eiē
pinein ainymenōi kai hoi potidorpion eiē.
sentences.l:
At once half, on the one hand, having curdled of the white milk
in woven baskets, having gathered it, he set down,
and half again he stood in vessels, so that for him it might be
to drink, when he took it, and for him for supper it might be.
sentences.i: At once he curdled half of the white milk, gathered it into woven baskets and set it down; the other half he stood in vessels, so that he would have it to drink when he took it, and it would serve as his supper as well.
sentences.n: ἥμισυ μὲν … ἥμισυ δ’ is 'half … and half', the milk divided in two. θρέψας is the aorist participle of τρέφω, which means 'nourish' but also 'thicken, curdle'; here it is 'having curdled', the half that becomes cheese, and ἀμησάμενος is 'having gathered it up', an aorist middle of ἀμάω. πλεκτοῖς ἐν ταλάροισιν is 'in woven baskets', ταλάροι being wicker baskets, and κατέθηκεν is 'he set down'. αὖτ’ is 'again', ἔστησεν 'made to stand', ἐν ἄγγεσιν 'in vessels' (as at 222). ὄφρα οἱ εἴη πίνειν is 'so that he might have it to drink', with αἰνυμένῳ 'taking it', a dative agreeing with οἱ; ποτιδόρπιον εἴη repeats the words of 234.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ σπεῦσε πονησάμενος τὰ ἃ ἔργα,
καὶ τότε πῦρ ἀνέκαιε καὶ εἴσιδεν, εἴρετο δ’ ἡμέας·
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē speuse ponēsamenos ta ha erga,
kai tote pyr anekaie kai eisiden, eireto d’ hēmeas·
sentences.l:
But when he had hurried, having toiled through his own tasks,
and then a fire he kindled and looked in, and he asked us:
sentences.i: But when he had hurried through his own tasks, he kindled the fire, caught sight of us, and asked:
sentences.n: τὰ ἃ ἔργα is 'his own tasks': ἅ is the possessive ὅς 'his own', neuter plural to agree with ἔργα, not the relative, and τά strengthens it. σπεῦσε is the aorist of σπεύδω 'hurry', with πονησάμενος 'having toiled through' (an aorist middle participle of πονέω). ἀνέκαιε 'he kindled', εἴσιδεν 'he looked in and saw' (an unaugmented aorist of εἰσοράω), and εἴρετο 'he asked' (an aorist middle of ἔρομαι) come one after the other, and ἡμέας is ἡμᾶς 'us'. The colon opens the Cyclops' first words, spoken inside Odysseus' own telling, so they carry single quotation marks.

sentences.t: ὦ ξεῖνοι, τίνες ἐστέ; πόθεν πλεῖθ’ ὑγρὰ κέλευθα;
sentences.tr: ō xeinoi, tines este; pothen pleith’ hygra keleutha;
sentences.l: ‘O strangers, who are you? From where do you sail the watery ways?
sentences.i: ‘Strangers, who are you? From where have you come sailing over the watery ways?
sentences.n: The Cyclops speaks, in words that Odysseus reports inside his own telling, so they carry single quotation marks. ξεῖνοι 'strangers' is from ξεῖνος, the word for stranger, guest and host alike, and the guest-host bond it names runs through the rest of this exchange. τίνες ἐστέ is 'who are you?'. πόθεν is 'from where?', with the suffix -θεν 'from'; πλεῖθ’ is πλεῖτε 'you sail', the τ roughened to θ before the rough breathing of ὑγρά, and ὑγρὰ κέλευθα 'the watery ways' is an accusative of the way sailed over. The two questions are the same as at 3.71, where Nestor puts them to Telemachus and his men.

sentences.l:
Is it on some business, or at random that you wander,
as pirates do over the salt-sea, who roam about,
staking their lives, bringing evil to men of other lands?’
sentences.i: Is it on some business, or are you roaming at random, as pirates do who wander over the sea, staking their lives and bringing harm to men of other lands?’
sentences.n: These three lines are the same as 3.72–74, and are translated the same way. ἦ τι κατὰ πρῆξιν is 'is it on some business?', κατά with the accusative giving the purpose, and ἦ μαψιδίως 'or at random'; ἀλάλησθε is the perfect of ἀλάομαι, 'you are wandering'. οἷά τε ληιστῆρες is 'as pirates do', with the epic τε for what is generally true; ὑπεὶρ ἅλα is 'over the salt-sea' (ὑπείρ = ὑπέρ), and τοί τ’ ἀλόωνται is 'who roam', τοί being a relative here. ψυχὰς παρθέμενοι is 'having staked their lives' (an aorist middle participle of παρατίθημι), and κακὸν … φέροντες 'bringing evil' takes the dative ἀλλοδαποῖσι 'to men of other lands'. The closing single mark ends the Cyclops' question.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἡμῖν δ’ αὖτε κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ,
δεισάντων φθόγγον τε βαρὺν αὐτόν τε πέλωρον.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hēmin d’ aute kateklasthē philon ētor,
deisantōn phthongon te baryn auton te pelōron.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and to us again was broken the dear heart,
of us having feared his voice, heavy, and the monster himself.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and our hearts broke within us again, in fear of his deep voice and of the monster himself.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ὣς ἔφατο 'so he spoke', the formula that closes a speech, the τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ἡμῖν. κατεκλάσθη is the aorist passive of κατακλάω 'break down', with φίλον ἦτορ 'the dear heart' as its subject and ἡμῖν 'to us' saying whose it was; αὖτε is 'again, in turn'. δεισάντων is a genitive plural aorist participle of δείδω, agreeing with an understood 'of us', 'as we feared', and φθόγγον τε βαρὺν αὐτόν τε πέλωρον 'his heavy voice and the monster himself' are its two objects. πέλωρον is a neuter noun, 'monster', from which πελώριος 'monstrous' is formed.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥς μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: alla kai hōs min epessin ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: But even so, with words, answering him, I addressed him:
sentences.i: But even so I answered him, and spoke:
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥς is 'but even so', the accented ὥς being the adverb 'thus'. μιν is 'him', ἔπεσσιν a dative plural 'with words', ἀμειβόμενος 'answering' and προσέειπον 'I addressed', the first-person form of the reply-formula that otherwise says 'he addressed'. The ano teleia opens Odysseus' speech to the Cyclops.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς τοι Τροίηθεν ἀποπλαγχθέντες Ἀχαιοὶ
παντοίοις ἀνέμοισιν ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης,
οἴκαδε ἱέμενοι, ἄλλην ὁδὸν ἄλλα κέλευθα
ἤλθομεν·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis toi Troiēthen apoplanchthentes Achaioi
pantoiois anemoisin hyper mega laitma thalassēs,
oikade hiemenoi, allēn hodon alla keleutha
ēlthomen·
sentences.l:
‘We, you know, from Troy driven off course, Achaeans,
by winds of every kind over the great gulf of the sea,
homeward eager, another road, other paths,
we came;
sentences.i: ‘We are Achaeans, I tell you, driven off course from Troy by winds of every kind across the great gulf of the sea; we were eager for home, but we came by another road, by other paths;
sentences.n: This is Odysseus' answer to the Cyclops, spoken inside his own telling, and so in single quotation marks. ἡμεῖς is 'we', with τοι 'I tell you' and Ἀχαιοί 'Achaeans' as the predicate. ἀποπλαγχθέντες is an aorist passive participle of ἀποπλάζω 'drive off course', παντοίοις ἀνέμοισιν 'by winds of every kind' is a dative of means, and ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης is 'over the great gulf of the sea'. Τροίηθεν has -θεν 'from' and Ionic η; οἴκαδε has -δε of direction, and ἱέμενοι means 'eager'. ἄλλην ὁδὸν ἄλλα κέλευθα ἤλθομεν is 'we came by another road, other paths', the accusatives naming the way travelled.

sentences.t: οὕτω που Ζεὺς ἤθελε μητίσασθαι.
sentences.tr: houtō pou Zeus ēthele mētisasthai.
sentences.l: so, I suppose, Zeus wished to devise.
sentences.i: so, I suppose, Zeus wished to plan it.
sentences.n: οὕτω is 'so, thus', and που 'I suppose': the speaker guesses at a cause he cannot know. Ζεύς is the subject, ἤθελε is 'wished' (the form ἤθελε beside ἔθελε), and μητίσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of μητίομαι 'devise, plan', built on μῆτις 'cunning, plan'; the object is not stated. The unit is the end of a line, cut off at the ano teleia after ἤλθομεν.

sentences.t:
λαοὶ δ’ Ἀτρεΐδεω Ἀγαμέμνονος εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι,
τοῦ δὴ νῦν γε μέγιστον ὑπουράνιον κλέος ἐστί·
sentences.tr:
laoi d’ Atreïdeō Agamemnonos euchometh’ einai,
tou dē nyn ge megiston hypouranion kleos esti·
sentences.l:
and people of Atreus’ son Agamemnon we declare ourselves to be,
of whom indeed now at least the greatest under-heaven fame is;
sentences.i: and we declare ourselves the men of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, whose fame is now the greatest under heaven;
sentences.n: λαοί are 'people', here the followers of a leader, his men. Ἀτρεΐδεω is a genitive in -εω 'of the son of Atreus', with Ἀγαμέμνονος in apposition. εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι is 'we declare ourselves to be': εὔχομαι means 'pray' and also 'declare, claim'. τοῦ is the relative 'of whom, whose', and δὴ νῦν γε is 'indeed now at least'. μέγιστον ὑπουράνιον κλέος is 'the greatest fame under heaven', with ὑπουράνιον 'under-the-sky' as an adjective.

sentences.t:
τόσσην γὰρ διέπερσε πόλιν καὶ ἀπώλεσε λαοὺς
πολλούς.
sentences.tr:
tossēn gar dieperse polin kai apōlese laous
pollous.
sentences.l:
for so great a city he sacked utterly and destroyed people
many.
sentences.i: for he sacked so great a city and destroyed many people.
sentences.n: τόσσην 'so great' agrees with πόλιν 'city', and γάρ gives the reason for the fame just claimed. διέπερσε is the aorist of διαπέρθω 'sack utterly', and ἀπώλεσε that of ἀπόλλυμι 'destroy'; λαούς 'people' is set apart from πολλούς 'many', which opens line 266 and ends the sentence at the full stop.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ αὖτε κιχανόμενοι τὰ σὰ γοῦνα
ἱκόμεθ’, εἴ τι πόροις ξεινήιον ἠὲ καὶ ἄλλως
δοίης δωτίνην, ἥ τε ξείνων θέμις ἐστίν.
sentences.tr:
hēmeis d’ aute kichanomenoi ta sa gouna
hikometh’, ei ti porois xeinēion ēe kai allōs
doiēs dōtinēn, hē te xeinōn themis estin.
sentences.l:
and we in turn, reaching your knees,
have come, if some guest-gift you might give, or even otherwise
might grant a present, which is the due of strangers.
sentences.i: and we, for our part, have come to your knees in case you might give a guest-gift, or in some other way grant a present, as is the due of strangers.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς δ’ αὖτε 'and we in turn' sets the Achaeans' own case beside Agamemnon's fame. κιχανόμενοι is a participle of κιχάνω 'reach, come to', and τὰ σὰ γοῦνα is 'your knees', the part of the body a suppliant clasps; ἱκόμεθ’ is 'we have come'. εἴ τι πόροις 'in case you might give' puts a hope in the optative, with ξεινήιον 'a guest-gift'; δοίης δωτίνην 'you might grant a present' is a second optative, with ἠὲ καὶ ἄλλως 'or even otherwise'. ἥ τε ξείνων θέμις ἐστίν is 'which is the due of strangers': ἥ is the relative, feminine like its antecedent δωτίνην and the predicate θέμις 'right, custom', and the epic τε marks a general rule.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ αἰδεῖο, φέριστε, θεούς·
sentences.tr: all’ aideio, pheriste, theous·
sentences.l: But respect, best of men, the gods;
sentences.i: But show respect, best of men, for the gods;
sentences.n: αἰδεῖο is the imperative middle of αἰδέομαι 'respect, show reverence for', and it takes θεούς 'the gods'. φέριστε is the vocative of φέριστος 'best', a courteous, even flattering address. The unit is only the first part of line 269; the speech goes on after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἱκέται δέ τοί εἰμεν,
Ζεὺς δ’ ἐπιτιμήτωρ ἱκετάων τε ξείνων τε,
ξείνιος, ὃς ξείνοισιν ἅμ’ αἰδοίοισιν ὀπηδεῖ.
sentences.tr:
hiketai de toi eimen,
Zeus d’ epitimētōr hiketaōn te xeinōn te,
xeinios, hos xeinoisin ham’ aidoioisin opēdei.
sentences.l:
and suppliants, you know, we are,
and Zeus is the avenger of suppliants and of strangers,
the guest-god, who with revered strangers keeps company.’
sentences.i: and we are, I tell you, your suppliants; and Zeus is the avenger of suppliants and of strangers, the god of guests, who keeps company with revered strangers.’
sentences.n: ἱκέται 'suppliants' is the predicate, with τοι 'I tell you', and εἰμεν is ἐσμέν 'we are'. Ζεύς has no verb: 'is' is understood. ἐπιτιμήτωρ 'avenger' is built on ἐπιτιμάω 'assign a penalty, punish', though its exact sense is not certain, and its genitives are ἱκετάων τε ξείνων τε 'of suppliants and of strangers', ἱκετάων having the epic -άων. ξείνιος is the adjective from ξεῖνος, 'of guests', the title of Zeus as god of the guest-bond; ὃς … ὀπηδεῖ is 'who keeps company with', taking the dative ξείνοισιν … αἰδοίοισιν 'revered strangers'. The repeated ξεῖν- rings through these lines. The closing single mark ends Odysseus' plea.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο νηλέι θυμῷ·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, ho de m’ autik’ ameibeto nēlei thymōi·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he then at once answered me with pitiless heart:
sentences.i: So I spoke, and he answered me at once, with a pitiless heart:
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην 'so I spoke' is the first-person counterpart of ὣς ἔφατο, closing Odysseus' own speech to the Cyclops, and ὁ δέ 'and he' has ὁ as a pronoun, μ’ being 'me'. αὐτίκ’ is 'at once', and ἀμείβετο 'answered' is ἠμείβετο without its augment. νηλέι θυμῷ 'with pitiless heart' is a dative of manner, νηλεής 'pitiless' being built on νη- 'not' and ἔλεος 'pity'. The colon opens the Cyclops' answer.

sentences.t:
νήπιός εἰς, ὦ ξεῖν’, ἢ τηλόθεν εἰλήλουθας,
ὅς με θεοὺς κέλεαι ἢ δειδίμεν ἢ ἀλέασθαι·
sentences.tr:
nēpios eis, ō xein’, ē tēlothen eilēlouthas,
hos me theous keleai ē deidimen ē aleasthai·
sentences.l:
‘A fool you are, stranger, or from far off you have come,
you who bid me the gods either to fear or to avoid;
sentences.i: ‘You are a fool, stranger, or else you have come from far away, you who tell me either to fear the gods or to avoid them;
sentences.n: νήπιός εἰς is 'you are a fool', εἰς being εἶ and νήπιος 'foolish, childish'. ὦ ξεῖν’ is 'stranger', ξεῖνε elided. ἢ 'or' opens a fork: he is a fool, or he comes from far off, τηλόθεν having -θεν 'from' and εἰλήλουθας being the perfect of ἔρχομαι 'you have come'. ὅς με … κέλεαι is 'you who bid me': ὅς is a relative with 'you' understood, and κέλεαι is the second person of κέλομαι 'urge, order'. θεοὺς … δειδίμεν is 'to fear the gods', ἢ … ἢ 'either … or' setting the two infinitives against each other, δειδίμεν being an infinitive of δείδω, and ἀλέασθαι 'to avoid', the aorist infinitive of ἀλέομαι, has the same object θεούς.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ Κύκλωπες Διὸς αἰγιόχου ἀλέγουσιν
οὐδὲ θεῶν μακάρων, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτεροί εἰμεν·
sentences.tr:
ou gar Kyklōpes Dios aigiochou alegousin
oude theōn makarōn, epei ē poly pherteroi eimen·
sentences.l:
for the Cyclopes take no heed of aegis-bearing Zeus
nor of the blessed gods, since indeed much stronger we are;
sentences.i: For the Cyclopes take no heed of aegis-bearing Zeus or of the blessed gods, since we are, in truth, far stronger;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ 'for … not' gives his reason. Κύκλωπες 'Cyclopes' is the subject of ἀλέγουσιν 'care for, pay heed to', which takes the genitives Διὸς αἰγιόχου 'aegis-bearing Zeus' (the meaning of αἰγίοχος is disputed) and θεῶν μακάρων 'blessed gods'; οὐδέ 'nor' carries the negative into the next line. ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτεροί εἰμεν is 'since indeed we are much stronger': ἦ is 'truly', φέρτεροι the comparative 'stronger, better', and εἰμεν = ἐσμέν. φέρτεροι is from the same root as φέριστε in 269.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν ἐγὼ Διὸς ἔχθος ἀλευάμενος πεφιδοίμην
οὔτε σεῦ οὔθ’ ἑτάρων, εἰ μὴ θυμός με κελεύοι.
sentences.tr:
oud’ an egō Dios echthos aleuamenos pephidoimēn
oute seu outh’ hetarōn, ei mē thymos me keleuoi.
sentences.l:
nor would I, Zeus’s enmity avoiding, spare
either you or your companions, unless my heart should bid me.
sentences.i: and I would not spare you or your companions to avoid the enmity of Zeus, unless my heart bade me.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἂν … πεφιδοίμην is 'nor would I spare': πεφιδοίμην is a reduplicated aorist optative of φείδομαι 'spare', a potential with ἂν. Διὸς ἔχθος ἀλευάμενος is 'avoiding the enmity of Zeus', ἀλευάμενος being the aorist middle participle of ἀλέομαι, the verb of ἀλέασθαι in 274, and ἔχθος 'hatred' its object. οὔτε σεῦ οὔθ’ ἑτάρων is 'neither you nor your companions', σεῦ being σοῦ, both genitives after πεφιδοίμην. εἰ μὴ θυμός με κελεύοι is 'unless my heart should bid me', the exception, with the optative κελεύοι; θυμός is plain 'heart' here.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι εἴφ’ ὅπῃ ἔσχες ἰὼν ἐυεργέα νῆα,
ἤ που ἐπ’ ἐσχατιῆς, ἦ καὶ σχεδόν, ὄφρα δαείω.
sentences.tr:
alla moi eiph’ hopēi esches iōn eyergea nēa,
ē pou ep’ eschatiēs, ē kai schedon, ophra daeiō.
sentences.l:
But to me tell where you stopped, coming, your well-made ship,
whether perhaps at the edge, or also near, so that I may learn.’
sentences.i: But tell me where you brought your well-made ship to a stop, whether at the edge or somewhere near, so that I may know.’
sentences.n: ἀλλά μοι εἴφ’ is 'but tell me': εἴφ’ is the aorist imperative εἰπέ, elided, the π turned to φ before the rough breathing of ὅπῃ. ὅπῃ ἔσχες ἰών is 'where you held (her) as you came': ἔσχες is the aorist of ἔχω, used of bringing a ship to a stop, and ἰών is the participle of εἶμι 'go'. ἐυεργέα νῆα is 'well-made ship', the adjective used of gold at 202. ἤ που … ἦ καὶ is 'whether perhaps … or even', with ἐπ’ ἐσχατιῆς 'at the edge' and σχεδόν 'near'. ὄφρα δαείω is 'so that I may learn', a subjunctive of δάω 'learn'. The closing single mark ends the Cyclops' speech; Odysseus' own telling, the speech of 9.2, goes on.
